stash:datasets.title: Data from:  The Duntulm sauropod tracksite and environmental partitioning in Middle Jurassic dinosaurs on the Isle of Skye, Scotland
stash:datasets.abstract: Dinosaur fossils from the Isle of Skye (Scotland, UK), particularly the abundant trace fossil record, provide a window into dinosaur evolution during the poorly known Middle Jurassic. Here we present the photogrammetric models, orthophotos, and underlying photosets and ground control points underpinning a comprehensive description of the Duntulm tracksite from Cairidh Ghlumaig Bay. We used this data to create whole site maps, catalogue the tracks, and identify trackways. The tracksite is dominated by small to medium-sized (<75 cm) sauropod footprints spanning several preservation styles, from casts with details of toes to impressions with less distinct features. Several short, narrow-gauge trackways indicate the sauropods were moving with a walking gait, and the wide range of orientations of the trackways does not indicate any gregarious behavior. Sparse, isolated theropod footprints are also present along the Duntulm coastline. We then examined the relationship between Skye's dinosaur trackmakers and the substrate in which the footprints are found. We found that Skye's sauropods had a preference for lagoonal substrates, while 'non-sauropod' dinosaurs (theropods, thyreophorans, and ornithopods) are more abundant in subaerially exposed mudflats.

funders.awardTitle: Philip Leverhulme Prize awarded to SLB

funders.organization: Derek and Maureen Moss and Richard Deveira

stash:datasets.methods: We used two unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) with payloads of cameras oriented at nadir to survey the main track-bearing platform at Duntulm. In total, we flew six flights at 6 m above the ground surface. We used the resulting 554 images to construct photogrammetric models of the Duntulm tracksite in Agisoft Metashape Version 1.8.4. This model was constrained with ground control points (GCPs) from relative carrier-phase GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) data collection with the reference station (Lochcarron – LCAR; ~60 km distance). The photogrammetric model and subsequent orthophotos were used for dinosaur footprint descriptions and measurements of trackway characteristics.

stash:datasets.title: Data and code from: Rapid evolution of body size in response to consistent natural selection in a wild lizard
stash:datasets.abstract: Although directional selection and additive genetic variance are frequently detected in wild populations, evolutionary responses are often weak or absent, giving rise to a “paradox of stasis.” To explore the relationship between selection and evolution, we used a pedigreed wild population of lizards (Anolis sagrei) to quantify natural selection, estimate additive genetic (co)variances, and track phenotypic and genetic change in adult body size while addressing several factors that could lead to evolutionary stasis. Selection via adult reproductive success consistently favored larger body size in both sexes and was stronger in males. Body size was heritable and genetically correlated with adult reproductive success in both sexes, indicating that selection acted on underlying additive genetic variance. Across five annual cohorts, mean phenotypic values and breeding values for body size increased in both sexes, exceeding expectations under genetic drift. This rapid evolutionary response was not obscured by several processes commonly invoked to explain stasis. For example, accounting for phenotypic skew strengthened expected responses, and prior viability selection on juveniles did not phenotypically or genetically oppose selection on adult body size. Our results show that rapid evolutionary change is detectable in the wild when directional selection is consistent, acts on additive genetic variance, and is not genetically opposed by early-life viability selection.

stash:datasets.title: Electrocardiographic screening for left atrial enlargement in dogs: Derivation and validation of an algorithm combining lead II P-wave duration and the Morris index
stash:datasets.abstract: Combining electrocardiographic measurements may improve identification of dogs requiring echocardiographic assessment. This retrospective diagnostic accuracy study derived a three-category algorithm in 150 dogs and evaluated it in 50 separate validation dogs. Three observers independently measured lead II P-wave duration and the V1 Morris index, with observer A providing the primary analysis. Left atrium-to-aorta ratio (LA/Ao) ≥1.6 was the primary outcome; normalized left ventricular internal diameter in diastole (LVIDDN) ≥1.7 was evaluated independently as a secondary outcome. Thresholds from 114 reference dogs were 48 and 52 ms for P duration and 3.04 mV·ms for Morris. Positive triage comprised intermediate and high categories. Primary-outcome sensitivity and specificity were 90.6% and 50.0% in derivation and 100% and 85.7% in validation. Validation sensitivity had a 95% confidence interval of 88.1%–100%. The ordinal algorithm area under the curve was 0.961 in validation, compared with 0.868 for P and 0.844 for Morris; paired differences were not significant after Holm adjustment. Secondary-outcome validation sensitivity and specificity were 88.0% and 60.0%. The algorithm provided complementary detection of left atrial enlargement and reproducible measurements across observers, supporting further evaluation as an adjunct to echocardiographic triage.
stash:datasets.methods:
Study population

Reporting was guided by STARD 2015 and STROBE-Vet recommendations (Bossuyt et al. 2015; Cohen et al. 2016; O’Connor et al. 2016). This retrospective diagnostic accuracy study included 150 dogs in a derivation cohort and 50 dogs in a separate validation cohort. Derivation examinations were performed at the veterinary diagnostic imaging center NUDIVE, Federal University of Piauí (UFPI), Brazil, between July 2024 and June 2025. Eligibility required a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and complete echocardiographic examination obtained on the same day. All 200 dogs were included in the principal analyses. The sample comprised the available eligible records; no prospective sample-size calculation was documented. American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine (ACVIM) stages were recorded using the consensus framework (Keene et al. 2019). The study was approved by the UFPI Animal Use Ethics Committee (CEUA/UFPI; protocol 824/2024), and written owner consent was obtained.

Electrocardiographic acquisition and measurements

ECGs were recorded with a digital 12-lead INCardio X system with dogs in right lateral recumbency without sedation, at 50 mm/s and 10 mm/mV, for 3 min. V1 placement followed the precordial lead system described by Santilli et al. (2019). Three observers, designated A, B, and C, independently measured the ECGs while blinded to the other readings and clinical and echocardiographic findings. When baseline instability, artifacts, or indistinct wave boundaries prevented reliable measurement, other readable regions of the same tracing were examined under the same blinding conditions.

Each stored ECG value represented the automatically generated mean of three measurements. Individual measurements were not retained; therefore, within-tracing repeatability could not be assessed. P-wave duration in lead II was expressed in milliseconds. The Morris index was calculated as the duration of the terminal negative P-wave component in V1 multiplied by its absolute amplitude, in mV·ms. Measurement of the terminal negative component and calculation of the index are illustrated in Fig. 1. P-wave termination was referenced to the isoelectric T–P baseline when the P–R segment was sloped. In derivation, the PR interval was calculated as lead II P duration plus the PR segment, and the Macruz index as P duration divided by the PR segment. PR and Macruz were ancillary variables and did not enter the algorithm.

Echocardiographic reference

One echocardiographer, blinded to ECG results, performed the reference examinations using a GE Vivid iq v203 system. LA/Ao was measured in early diastole in the right parasternal short-axis view at the aortic valve level, following the ACVIM approach (Keene et al. 2019). LA/Ao ≥1.6 defined the primary outcome of left atrial enlargement. Left ventricular internal diameter in diastole (LVIDd), LVIDDN, and peak early diastolic transmitral E velocity were measured by the same echocardiographer. LVIDDN was calculated as LVIDd in centimeters divided by body weight in kilograms raised to 0.294 (Cornell et al. 2004). LVIDDN ≥1.7 defined the secondary outcome, independently of LA/Ao. A single reference examination was shared by all ECG observers for each dog.

Data management and algorithm derivation

Records were matched by animal identifier. Checks included completeness, duplicate identifiers, agreement of shared echocardiographic measurements, consistency of derived variables, and the relationship between terminal V1 duration and total P duration in lead II. Each dog contributed one stored value per variable and observer. No principal measurement was imputed. Observer A provided the primary diagnostic analysis; B and C were evaluated separately without averaging ECG readings across observers.

The reference subgroup comprised derivation dogs in ACVIM stages A or B1 with LA/Ao <1.6. Empirical type 7 quantiles from observer A defined the 70th and 90th percentiles of P duration and the 70th percentile of Morris. The resulting decision rule assigned score 2 when P ≥52 ms or when P ≥48 ms and Morris ≥3.04 mV·ms; score 0 required P <48 ms and Morris <3.04 mV·ms; all other combinations received score 1 (Fig. 2). Categories were termed low, intermediate and high and represented increasing electrical evidence of enlargement, rather than predicted future events. Scores 1–2 defined positive triage, equivalent to P ≥48 ms or Morris ≥3.04 mV·ms. Score 2 alone was assessed as a more selective operating point. All thresholds were fixed for validation, other observers and the secondary outcome.

Statistical analysis

Continuous characteristics were summarized using medians and interquartile ranges; counts and percentages described categorical variables. Diagnostic performance included sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, accuracy and likelihood ratios. Proportions received exact Clopper–Pearson 95% confidence intervals (CIs) (Clopper and Pearson 1934); likelihood-ratio intervals used the log approximation when estimable. Receiver operating characteristic analysis used the ordinal score and continuous P and Morris values. Areas under the curve (AUCs), CIs, and within-cohort paired comparisons were calculated using DeLong covariance estimates (DeLong et al. 1988). Between-cohort results were described separately.

Paired proportions were compared within McNemar’s framework (McNemar 1947), using two-sided exact conditional tests for sensitivity among outcome-positive dogs, specificity among outcome-negative dogs, and accuracy among all dogs. This implementation controls the nominal type I error rate but can be conservative and have reduced power (Fagerland et al. 2013). Holm adjustment was applied to the three marker pairs within each cohort, observer, outcome, and metric (Aickin and Gensler 1996). Associations between categories and outcomes were assessed with the Fisher–Freeman–Halton exact test; pairwise category comparisons used Fisher exact tests with Holm adjustment. B and C underwent the same analyses against the shared reference. Paired observer comparisons used corresponding three-comparison families. All tests were two-sided; adjusted p <0.05 indicated statistical evidence within the specified family.

Between-observer agreement of stored P and Morris means was assessed using the two-way absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficient for a single observer value, ICC(A,1) (McGraw and Wong 1996; Koo and Li 2016). Confidence intervals were estimated using 3,000 dog-level bootstrap samples, with complete observer sets retained during resampling (Efron 1979). Bland–Altman bias and limits of agreement were calculated for each observer pair (Bland and Altman 1986). Linear-weighted kappa assessed ordinal scores (Cohen 1968), and unweighted kappa assessed triage decisions (Cohen 1960). Friedman and paired Wilcoxon tests examined observer differences (Friedman 1937; Wilcoxon 1945).

An exploratory stratified five-fold derivation check re-estimated thresholds within each training reference subgroup and applied them to held-out dogs. This internal check evaluated the development procedure within the available derivation sample, consistent with the distinction between apparent performance and performance assessed by resampling (Steyerberg et al. 2001). Additional analyses included ancillary PR/Macruz discrimination, descriptive Spearman correlations, and exploratory net benefit of fixed referral strategies (Vickers and Elkin 2006; Vickers et al. 2019). Supplementary methods, tables and figures provide complete specifications and results.[1]

Analyses were performed in Python 3.12.14 with NumPy 2.3.5, pandas 2.2.3, SciPy 1.17.0, and scikit-learn 1.8.0; figures were produced with Matplotlib 3.10.8. Code, exact package versions, and the random seed (20260910) are provided with the data.

[1] Supplementary methods, Tables S1–S8, Figures S1–S4 and the data and code archive accompany this article.

stash:datasets.title: Data and code from: Dispersal-limited birds at high risk from cattle farming deforestation in tropical forests
stash:datasets.abstract: We explore the question: how do farming activities affect functional diversity and species traits across different spatial scales in tropical forests? This dataset uses outputs from multispecies occupancy models from Socolar and Mills et al. (2025) to estimate avian communities across 13 different biogeographic units at near-national scales in Colombia. We quantify changes in functional diversity resulting from forest-to-pasture conversion and identify the most impacted functional dimension. Includes computing occupancy community-weighted means, regression modelling of occupancy change across functional dimensions, and cumulative changes in functional metrics at increasing scales. Results indicate that functional diversity metrics are only slightly affected across ecoregions and largely reflect the national scale of loss, driven by a moderate reduction in Functional Richness across scales. particularly affects birds with functional traits related to low dispersal capability.

stash:datasets.title: Blow fly sampling in Southern California, 2022-2023

affiliations.organization: John Jay College of Criminal Justice

stash:datasets.abstract: This dataset includes blow fly (Diptera: Calliphoridae) communities across four ecoregions in Southern California, and local environmental conditions measured using data loggers or nearby weather stations. Collected between 2022 and 2023, the dataset includes collection date, seasonal classification, environmental variables (temperature and relative humidity), trap duration, geographic location (latitude, longitude, ecoregion), and detailed species data (sex-specific and total counts). Environmental data were sourced from HOBO loggers or weather stations and aligned with sampling events. These data support investigations of metacommunity structure, particularly the roles of environmental filtering and dispersal across spatial scales. The dataset enables reuse in studies of necrophagous insect ecology, climate change impacts, and biodiversity monitoring in fragmented landscapes. No personally identifiable or ethically sensitive information is included. Users should cite the dataset when used and consult associated publications for methodological context and analytical frameworks.

stash:datasets.title: Data from: Divergent mandibular morphology in American mink (Neogale vison) fossils suggests novel role in past environments
stash:datasets.abstract: Understanding the presence and spatial distribution of intraspecific morphological variation may shed light on the natural history and ecological breadth, realized and potential, of specific taxa. Insights from the paleontological record can provide additional information on potential phenotypic variation for species that have adapted to past and present environments. Here, we use the American mink (Neogale vison) as a case study to understand the extent and pattern of mandibular shape variation among extant populations (n = 290) and fossil assemblages (n = 13). We placed geometric morphometric landmarks and semilandmarks on 3D models generated from laser light scans of mandibles. A subset of specimens were landmarked in triplicate to assess error. We found that some fossil N. vison mandibles lie outside the morphospace occupied by extant N. vison and are distinct from modern mink. Fossils from Conard Fissure, Arkansas (n = 8) represent a unique morphotype that likely had higher bite forces than modern N. vison. This morphotype may have allowed N. vison at this site to take advantage of larger or different prey. These results demonstrate both the adaptive potential of N. vison and the fossil record’s ability to reveal unique variation in a lineage.

stash:datasets.title: Data from: Lessons from a prioritisation process to identify evidence needs at the Woodland Trust, UK
stash:datasets.abstract:
Despite growing acknowledgement and advocacy for the importance of evidence-based conservation, there remain several challenges for conservation organisations to achieve this in reality. Misaligned incentives between academic research and conservation practice can limit the relevance, applicability and accessibility of research. A further challenge is the low number of practitioner-led research agendas that are published with which academics can engage and enable academic-practitioner co-designed research.

To address this challenge, 149 employees from the Woodland Trust were consulted in a series of facilitated workshops and surveys to produce a practitioner-led research agenda. First, an online survey and consultation meetings took place to gather research and evidence questions. Second, subject matter experts collated and synthesised these questions. Third, workshops were run to refine and score research questions using the criteria of overall priority, urgency, and an identifiable pathway to apply research output in conservation practice.

The results of this process are presented in this dataset which includes 173 applied conservation research questions across 14 topic areas and their relative prioritisation score. 

We encourage academics and other researchers working in the sector to review this research agenda and contact the Woodland Trust research team to discuss co-designing future research projects or share current available evidence that addresses research questions within the agenda.

For further information please contact: research@woodlandtrust.org.uk

stash:datasets.title: Data from: Mimicry disparity in ant-mimicking spiders using an avian visual model
stash:datasets.abstract: Batesian mimicry is a widespread evolutionary strategy in which palatable species gain protection by resembling defended models, yet mimetic systems often vary substantially in accuracy. Ant mimicry (myrmecomorphy) is a prominent example, occurring across diverse arthropod lineages and ecological contexts. However, how variation in resemblance is structured across visual traits and environments remains poorly understood from a predator-centred perspective. We examined perceptual similarity between 16 ant-mimicking spiders and their putative ant models from Ndumo Game Reserve, South Africa, and included non-co-occurring ant species to place focal comparisons within broader patterns of ant colour variation. Using avian visual modelling, we quantified chromatic and achromatic contrasts across body regions in spiders (prosoma and opisthosoma) and ants (head plus thorax and abdomen). Similarity varied among species pairs and visual channels; some associations showed close chromatic resemblance but weaker achromatic similarity. Body region had little influence on perceptual distance, whereas exploratory analyses suggested habitat context may contribute to variation in mimetic similarity in spiders but not model ants. Overall, ant mimicry shows trait- and context-dependent variation in perceptual similarity. This supports the view that imperfect mimicry reflects a widespread, evolutionarily stable outcome of selection acting across multiple traits and perceptual channels.
stash:datasets.methods: The data contained in this dataset can be used to replicate all analyses that are detailed in the manuscript: Mimicry disparity in ant-mimicking spiders using an avian visual model.

stash:datasets.title: Data and code from: Mating triggers a physiological switch to reproduction in field crickets to mitigate the flight-oogenesis tradeoff
stash:datasets.abstract: Organisms must reallocate limited resources to meet changing physiological demands, yet the cues that trigger these shifts and the physiological programs that mediate them remain poorly understood. For example, in some winged animals, females cannot simultaneously invest in energetically expensive flight musculature and egg production, requiring physiological transitions between dispersal and reproductive phases of their life cycle (the flight-oogenesis trade-off). However, the mechanisms that allow individuals to transition between dispersal and reproductive states remain unclear. Here, we test whether mating acts as a key external cue that reprograms internal resource allocation from somatic maintenance to reproduction. Using the wing-dimorphic California variable field cricket, Gryllus lineaticeps, we show that mating initiates flight muscle histolysis in long-winged females, eliminating any delay in early-life fecundity. Mating activates transcriptional programs associated with autophagy, iron mobilization, and endocrine signaling, consistent with a coordinated physiological shift that redirects nutrients from flight tissues to oogenesis. These mating-induced changes include altered insulin-like peptide and juvenile hormone signaling, suggesting that conserved hormonal pathways may be repurposed to govern life-history transitions. Together, our findings reveal that mating can serve as a potent trigger for reorganizing nutrient use and physiological priorities, enabling organisms to minimize the reproductive costs of non-reproductive states. By identifying a socially derived cue that initiates state transitions, this work provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how reproductive behaviors drive life-history strategies, and challenges long-standing assumptions about the inherent costs of dispersal.

stash:datasets.title: Taphonomic and supplement data for: Quantification and mitigation of taphonomic biases in multi-taxon marine fossil assemblages using a mass-based, fragment-inclusive sampling approach
stash:datasets.abstract: Here we propose a fragment-inclusive mass-based (FIMB) approach to mitigate taphonomic biases and improve quantitative estimates of faunal composition in paleoecological studies. Using sympatric assemblages of irregular echinoids and shell-bearing mollusks collected from contemporary, shallow-water seafloors across four regions ([1] Carrabelle, Florida; [2] Cedar Key, Florida; [3] Curaçao, Netherlands Antilles; [4] Florida Keys, Florida), we tested the hypothesis that FIMB produces less biased estimates of faunal composition than traditional fragment-exclusionary (complete specimens only) mass or count-based approaches. We also tested two auxiliary taphonomic hypotheses, implied by the expected lower preservational potential of irregular echinoids compared to sympatric mollusks: (1) Irregular echinoid tests fragment more frequently than mollusk shells; (2) Whole specimen live-dead proportions are higher for irregular echinoids than for mollusks. Results support both taphonomic hypotheses, with irregular echinoids exhibiting higher fragmentation estimates and live-dead proportions than sympatric mollusks. However, both taxa are well represented by fragments. Consequently, the FIMB approach provides estimates of relative abundance of echinoids that better approximate their relative abundance in live assemblages. In contrast, traditional fragment-exclusionary approaches indicated that irregular echinoids were either absent or at most extremely rare in death assemblages. Our results demonstrate that although the FIMB approach offers lower taxonomic resolution than the methods based entirely on whole specimens, the fragment-inclusive method improves estimates of faunal composition by mitigating pronounced taphonomic biases that can affect multi-taxic assemblages.

stash:datasets.abstract: This dataset contains the source data supporting the study “A eukaryotic-like phospholipid transfer protein conserved in Asgard archaea.” The dataset is provided as a single Excel workbook organized into separate worksheets corresponding to each main Figure, Extended Data Figure, and Supplementary Figure. Additional worksheets contain the reference outputs generated with ProtDomRetriever (“ProtDomRetriever Results Ref”), the accession numbers and cavity size values associated with each extracted protein domain (“Domain Cavity Size Ref”), and the nucleotide primer sequences used in the study (“nt_primers_list”). The data include the numerical values underlying the quantitative analyses and graphical representations presented in the article and its supplementary material. The dataset can be reused to reproduce the reported quantitative analyses and graphical representations, and to inspect the underlying values associated with the reported results. No human participants, personal data, or other ethically sensitive information are included in this dataset.

stash:datasets.title: Data and code from: Substrate-dependent variation in environmental DNA persistence and degradation from a small mammal
stash:datasets.abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) analyses have been applied to terrestrial environments for over a decade, yet knowledge of the dynamics of eDNA deposition, movement, and degradation remains limited. To address this, we conducted a controlled experiment over one year to assess the persistence of eDNA from an arboreal mammal across four substrates (water, sediment, sheltered nest-box surfaces, and exposed nest-box surfaces). Environmental DNA deposited by captive individuals was sampled repeatedly following removal of animals and analysed using both species-specific qPCR and metabarcoding. We modelled degradation using quantitative decay, detection probability, and conditional decay frameworks, and applied a random breakage model to estimate theoretical fragment persistence. Decay followed first-order exponential kinetics in water and on nest box surfaces but not in sediment, which exhibited high stochasticity. We observed a large difference in degradation rates between substrates, with exponential decay models revealing half-lives ranging from 7.3 days in water to 276 days on sheltered internal surfaces. Rapid decay in water restricted detections to approximately 77 days, while persistence models predicted that sheltered surfaces could retain detectable DNA for more than four years (>1,700 days), indicating the potential for prolonged accumulation of legacy DNA in protected environments. While species-specific qPCR offered higher sensitivity than metabarcoding, both methods had parallel decay patterns. Our findings indicate that substrate selection is a critical decision when designing an eDNA survey, as there is a trade-off between maximising detection probability and maintaining temporal resolution.

stash:datasets.abstract:
This dataset provides the experimental data supporting a study on controllable phase shifts realized with colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) coupled to a hybrid microcavity at room temperature. The deposited files include the measured raw data, such as spectral data, interference data recorded at various probe wavelengths, and interference data measured under different pump powers.

The dataset relates to a platform in which a dielectric photonic-crystal-based hybrid microcavity is strongly coupled with CQDs, including both a single CQD positioned by a soft nano-probe technique and a high-concentration CQD ensemble. Combining photoluminescence spectroscopy, Michelson interferometry, and continuous-wave pump–probe measurements, the dataset records the phase response of the coupled system as a function of probe wavelength and pump power. Controlled π phase shifts at the single-photon level were obtained in both the single-CQD and high-concentration CQD systems. These data are intended to support the analysis and reproduction of the reported phase-shift behavior, and may be useful for the development of room-temperature quantum optoelectronic devices, such as quantum phase gates and low-power optical switches.

funders.organization: National Natural Science Foundation of China
Quantum Science and Technology-National Science and Technology Major Project

stash:datasets.methods:
Experimental Setup

The phase shifts of a strongly coupled colloidal quantum dot (CQD)–photonic crystal (PC) Fabry–Pérot (FP) cavity system were characterized using a Michelson-type interferometric setup combined with a continuous-wave (CW) pump–probe scheme. A 532 nm CW laser served as the pump, which generated a steady-state exciton population in the CQDs and provided a stable means of controlling the strength of the light–matter interaction in the coupled system. A tunable CW laser, operating between 735 and 830 nm, was used as the probe, with its power kept at the single-photon level (3–5 nW) so that the system state was not perturbed. This strong-pump/weak-probe configuration is well suited to examining the steady-state nonlinear response of the exciton–photon system.

Optical Path Configuration

The probe beam was divided by a beam splitter into a sample arm and a reference arm. In the sample arm, the probe was focused onto the sample surface through a 100× microscope objective, and the reflected beam, which carried the phase information modulated by the coupled system, was directed back along the same path. In the reference arm, the beam was reflected by a mirror mounted on a high-precision motorized translation stage. Scanning this stage continuously varied the reference optical path length, thereby introducing a controllable phase delay. The two returning beams were recombined at the beam splitter; residual pump light was removed with a filter, and the interference signal was detected by a silicon photodetector together with a lock-in amplifier to improve the measurement sensitivity.

Measurement Procedure

For each measurement, the piezoelectric translation stage was scanned to produce a stable interference fringe pattern. The microscope objective was adjusted so that the probe was focused on the core test unit of the sample, and the translation stage was driven to match the optical path lengths of the two arms, ensuring stable interference fringes. The interference fringes recorded with and without the pump beam were fitted with a sinusoidal function; the fitted phases were then extracted, and their difference gave the pump-induced phase shift.

To characterize the spectral response, the pump beam was switched off, and the relative phase shift was recorded as a function of probe wavelength over the range of 735–830 nm. This allowed the anomalous dispersion region associated with strong coupling to be identified and the optimal probe wavelength for the subsequent power-dependent measurements to be determined. For the power-dependent measurements, the probe wavelength was fixed at a selected value, the pump power was varied, and the corresponding phase shift was recorded. The average pump photon number was derived from the measured pump power using the cavity parameters. All measurements were carried out at room temperature.

Data Processing

For the phase measurements, the reference optical path length was varied in the lateral direction by a precision motorized scanning stage, and the resulting signal was combined with the direct signal to extract the interference information. A full scan of the stage covered multiple periods, which allowed multiple data points to be fitted. The data points shown in the main text were obtained by repeatedly scanning the piezoelectric stage while the pump power was increased incrementally. Using this multi-period, repeated-accumulation procedure together with subsequent curve fitting, the controlled phase shift as a function of pump power displayed a bi-exponential dependence. For measurements at different wavelengths and pump powers, the same repeated multi-period measurement and fitting procedure consistently yielded a bi-exponential trend characteristic of nonlinear interactions, confirming the reproducibility of the controlled phase-shift behavior.
